releases.name: Principled P.E.K.K.A
releases.headline: Principled P.E.K.K.A — your score now explains itself
notes: Hey —
Elixir Drop has a new named release: Principled P.E.K.K.A. It's three weeks of work, and the theme is Drop showing its own workings instead of asking you to trust them.

Your score now explains itself. If you post a run fast enough to get looked at, it still ranks while it's being checked. It just wears an Awaiting seal and says so on its row — no more scores quietly vanishing with no explanation. Only a run a referee actually excludes leaves the board, and if that ever happens to you, you get a plain-English reason and a short run tag you can email us about. Most games are never reviewed at all and carry no mark, because a Cleared seal should mean a person genuinely looked at that exact run.
One card changed cost. Void is now five elixir in Drop, correcting it to its real cost. If you'd learned it at the old number, that's why it suddenly feels wrong.

Your profile got rebuilt. There's a single "Your games" list now: filter by season, mode, or review status, grouped by month, marking your personal bests and where each one placed. Your arena, XP, and lifetime games sit up top. Seasons are named the way you'd say them out loud — Season 135, not a date code.

Your clan is on the board. Save your Clash Royale player tag and Drop finds your clan from your public profile, then ranks you against your clanmates on a board of their own. Tapping any name on a leaderboard now opens that player's profile. The boards themselves were rebuilt — fewer bands before the first row, modes shown as their own artwork, and times down to the millisecond, which is what the tiebreak was quietly using all along.

Badges. Twenty-nine of them, across speed, volume, consistency, and a few secrets. They're ladders rather than one-offs, they count games you'd already played before they existed, and the ones you earn can be shared as artwork.

The games got their real numbers. Rain is endless and speeds up. Survival, Trade, and Higher/Lower were rebalanced to their documented curves. Practice became a true drill — no clock, no ranks, no XP, just reps. And if you play fast, there's a Speedrun keyboard setting that deals the number pad as two wide rows, because mistaps happen sideways.
A different game is featured every day. All five ranked games now sit in one row that never reorders, and one of them takes the spotlight each day.

If you've installed Drop to your home screen, this release is noticeably smoother: card art caches as you play, the installed cache got smaller, dropped taps on the iOS keypad are fixed, and game layouts no longer break on short screens.
You can read the whole history any time at Drop → You → Releases.
Go see where you land: https://drop.poapkings.com
— Run by POAP KINGS

releases.name: Rallied Royal Recruits
releases.headline: Rallied Royal Recruits — the clan shows up on the board
notes: The beta that connected Drop to the clan. Save your Clash Royale player tag and Drop reads your public profile to find your clan, then ranks you against your clanmates on a board of their own.
Public player profiles picked up Clash identity, so a name on a leaderboard leads somewhere real.

Installed players got the biggest reliability pass yet: card art now caches progressively across modes, the installed art cache shrank, decode gaps were closed, and a broken cache upgrade handoff was fixed. App diagnostics landed for when something still goes wrong.
Podium badges started awarding at season rollover, and Sharp Trade and Clean Sweep were recalibrated against real play.

releases.name: Gilded Golem
releases.headline: Gilded Golem — Drop gets a face, and badges to chase
notes: The beta where Drop stopped borrowing its look. Artwork arrived for all six game modes, the app icon at eight sizes, badge medallions, empty-state illustrations, countdown frames, and share images — a complete visual system instead of emoji standing in for art.

Badges shipped behind it: ladders across speed, volume, consistency, and a few secrets. Each one is a counter and a set of rungs rather than a single trophy, they count games you had already played, and they never take an achievement back.
Earned badges became shareable as real artwork, player progression was polished around them, and game startup transitions were unified so every mode begins the same way.

releases.name: Measured Musketeer
releases.headline: Measured Musketeer — every game gets its real numbers
notes: The beta that stopped the games running on guesswork. Higher/Lower got three lives and a difficulty ramp tied to the elixir gap between the two cards. Trade opened on three straight 1v1 reads and followed a fixed ladder from there. Survival was pinned to its documented curve, and Rain was bounded by its own spawn curve and given a real tiebreak.
Practice was rebuilt as what its name promises: an endless, non-competitive drill with no clock, no ranking, and no XP, so there is somewhere to just learn.

Drop's fastest players asked for a Speedrun keyboard — the number pad dealt as two wide rows instead of one narrow one, because mistaps happen sideways. It is off by default and applies everywhere the pad appears.

The phone got a round of fixes that were overdue: dropped iOS keypad taps, game layouts breaking on short viewports, Higher/Lower taking a life the player never lost, and lives finally rendered as one shared hearts row.
This is also where the in-app Releases page appeared, which is why you can read any of this.

releases.name: Radiant Royal Giant
releases.headline: Meet Radiant Royal Giant — Drop's first named release
notes: Drop has its first named release: Radiant Royal Giant.

What began as a quick way to drill card costs is now a full game with six ways to play: Surge, Practice, Higher / Lower, Trade, Survival, and Rain. Sign in with a magic link to keep your progress, earn Player XP, climb a 28-arena journey, chase season bests, and see how your ranked runs stack up.

This release also brings a cleaner mobile and desktop experience, install support for your phone, keyboard controls on desktop, easier score sharing, and a long list of gameplay fixes and polish. Practice stays unranked and focused on learning; the other modes are ready when you want to race the board.
And if you need a quieter moment after the sprint, there is a card-rain screensaver hiding in plain sight.
Come give Radiant Royal Giant a run — and see which elixir cost still catches you.

releases.name: Prime Phoenix
releases.headline: Prime Phoenix — Drop gets rebuilt around the phone
notes: The beta that rebuilt Drop's shell from scratch. The site split into a proper mobile experience and a fixed desktop layout instead of one design stretched across both.

Rain arrived as a real ranked game rather than only a screensaver, complete with a higher/lower hint after a miss. Drop also became installable: add it to your home screen and it runs fullscreen on iOS, with signing in handled across that separate window.
About, FAQ, and Install pages showed up for the first time, score sharing moved front and centre, player profiles filled in, and desktop play picked up keyboard input.
Behind the scenes this is where the test suite went from thin to serious — automated coverage of real gameplay climbed from 30% to 83%, which is why the releases after it moved faster.

releases.name: Valiant Valkyrie
releases.headline: Valiant Valkyrie — competition becomes the point
notes: The beta that made Drop competition-first. Ranked play was standardized across the games, and the lineup was cut back to the modes that earned their place — with Practice deliberately pulled out of the competition entirely so it could just be practice.

Player XP landed as a measure of how much you play rather than how well, so a beginner always moves forward, and it drives a 28-arena climb of your own. All-time leaderboards joined the seasonal boards.
Guest play arrived too: try any game without an account. Sessions stretched to 28 days so signing in stopped being a chore.

Higher / Lower got its shrinking response clock and its tap-the-higher-card shape, Survival got a real clear-the-deck win, and the Elixir Rain screensaver appeared as an Easter egg for anyone who found it.

releases.name: Gallant Golden Knight
releases.headline: Gallant Golden Knight — accounts, leaderboards, and the clan beta
notes: The beta that turned Drop from a solo drill into something the clan could actually compete on. Sign in with a magic link, pick a favorite card, and keep a profile that follows you between devices.

Leaderboards went live, wired to the real Clan Wars clock so seasons line up with the game. Every run now comes from a signed server challenge, which is what makes a posted score mean anything — and implausible results get held back for review rather than sitting on the board.
Your Clash Royale profile can be linked for context, and account deletion and a plain-spoken privacy commitment shipped in the same stretch, because asking for an email means owing you a way out.
The learning stats that track which costs catch you moved to the server, and the interface picked up a consistent icon set.

releases.name: Humble Hog Rider
releases.headline: Humble Hog Rider — the first playable Drop
notes: Where Drop started: a browser game for learning Clash Royale elixir costs, built around the real card catalog.

Practice came first, then Surge as a timed sprint, then Higher / Lower, Trade, and Survival. Several other experiments rode along in this stretch and were later retired once it was clear which ones were actually fun.
Everything lived on your own device — no accounts, no leaderboards, no scores to defend. Just the cards, a summary at the end of each run, and a read on which costs you kept missing.
Sound, reduced-motion support, and settings were in from the start.
